claims.text: A physics-informed, data-driven machine-learning model will predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than conventional empirical or simplified ab initio methods.
The proposed model integrates high-throughput ab initio phonon calculations with disorder-sensitive descriptors.
Local bond environments, mass variance, and force-constant fluctuations are descriptors relevant to phonon transport in HEAs.
Multi-element disorder affects phonon scattering in HEAs.
Traditional predictive approaches tend to average out or neglect the effects of multi-element disorder.
The target materials are equimolar or near-equimolar HEAs with extensive chemical disorder.
High-throughput computational screening is useful for exploring the large compositional space of HEAs.
Phonon scattering dominates heat transport in HEAs at approximately 300–600 °C.
Localized compositional fluctuations and bond-strength variations drive phonon-scattering events.
Training on a large dataset of ab initio phonon calculations enables the model to capture diverse HEA phonon-scattering mechanisms.
Including configurational-disorder-sensitive descriptors reduces prediction error relative to methods that assume a uniform lattice.
The proposed model will predict experimental thermal conductivity within a 10–15% error margin.
The proposed model will identify HEAs with ultra-low phonon thermal conductivity more reliably than current methods.
Existing empirical correlations and simplified ab initio approaches neglect the full impact of multi-element disorder.
The expected predictive improvement primarily applies to single-phase, chemically disordered, equimolar or near-equimolar HEAs.
The predictive improvement may not extend to alloys dominated by phase separation or severe short-range order.
A deviation greater than 20% between measured and predicted phonon thermal conductivity would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to consistently identify compositions with lower thermal conductivity than those selected by conventional methods would falsify the hypothesis.
